analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans covering prescriptions to also cover fills at any pharmacy, with equal copays.
analysis.headline: The Prescription Drug Patient Choice Act of 1998, with zero cosponsors, was referred to four House committees and died there without a hearing or vote when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any health plan that covers prescription drugs only through its own network of contracted pharmacies to also let patients get prescriptions filled at out-of-network pharmacies, at the same premium, copay, and reimbursement terms. It would have applied to employer plans, individual insurance, Medicare and Medicaid managed care, Medigap policies, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits program. It was introduced in September 1998 and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People with prescription drug coverage through employer plans, individual insurance, Medicare or Medicaid managed care, Medigap, or the federal employees program who want to fill prescriptions at a pharmacy outside their plan's network — often a local independent pharmacy near home — at the same copay as a network pharmacy. Independent and community pharmacies would gain, since plans could not exclude them or reimburse them less.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients using out-of-network pharmacies; independent drugstores

how_it_helps.text: If a plan covers prescription drugs only through network pharmacies, it must also offer coverage for drugs filled at non-network pharmacies [S2][S3].
Plans could not charge higher premiums, copayments, or deductibles for using a non-network pharmacy, and had to reimburse non-network pharmacies at least as much as network ones [S2][S3].

The protections would have extended across nearly every type of coverage: employer plans under ERISA, the individual market, Medicare managed care, Medicaid managed care (with waivers prohibited), Medigap and Medicare Select policies, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and pharmacy benefit managers that run closed pharmacy networks would lose their ability to steer drug coverage to contracted pharmacies, giving up a cost-control tool; higher premiums for some enrollees could follow, since plans often use narrow networks to negotiate lower prices.

drawbacks.text: Banning higher copays and mandating equal reimbursement for out-of-network pharmacies would remove a plan's main lever for negotiating drug prices through networks, which could raise premiums for all enrollees [S3].

The bill was loosely drafted: its effective dates reach back to January 1, 1998, before its September 1998 introduction, its FEHBP section contains a garbled, unfinished sentence, and it would have disrupted some collectively bargained plans mid-contract [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — same copay at the pharmacy you actually use — is a real consumer win for people in closed networks, especially rural patients and independent-pharmacy customers. But the bill prices choice at zero: by forbidding any cost difference for out-of-network fills, it takes away plans' cheapest cost-control tool and likely shifts costs into premiums for everyone. And the drafting was careless enough (retroactive 1998 effective date, a broken sentence in the FEHBP section) that it shows the bill was a statement of position rather than a law anyone expected to pass.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the closing weeks of the session and sent to four committees, none of which ever held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on September 14, 1998, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to four committees — Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Government Reform — for the parts each oversees [S5].
In the following week it was sent to two subcommittees, the Civil Service subcommittee on September 17 and the Health and Environment subcommittee on September 21 [S5].
No committee acted further, no vote was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and pharmacy-benefit networks came out ahead: because the bill never moved, their closed pharmacy networks and the cost control they provide stayed untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and HMO pharmacy networks

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 14, 1998; no other member signed on as a cosponsor

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; its Health and Environment subcommittee received the bill September 21 and took no action

against.name: Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Government Reform committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 14, 1998 and took no recorded action on it

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor schedule in the final weeks of the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed no vote on the bill, consistent with the leadership's broader resistance to new managed-care regulation in 1998

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split can be measured; the only support in the record was one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have barred plans from charging more for prescriptions filled outside their contracted pharmacy networks, taking away a key tool for steering patients to network pharmacies. Since no action was ever taken, insurers' network arrangements continued unchanged.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and closed pharmacy networks
industries.note: Their contracts derive value from being the exclusive covered channel for prescriptions; the bill would have forced plans to pay non-network pharmacies equally and offer them as an option. The bill's death preserved their position.

Pharmacies outside plan networks would have gained the right to serve covered patients at equal reimbursement, restoring customers who are currently pushed toward network chains. The bill never advanced, so their disadvantage persisted.
